entries.topic: Withdrawals, disengagements and treaties 1974-2023, and the critics' reply

claims.text: Israel-Syria disengagement agreement signed in Geneva 31 May 1974: Israeli forces withdraw west of Line A except in the Kuneitra area (Line A-1); all territory east of Line A under Syrian administration and Syrian civilians return; UNDOF (about 1,200) in the separation zone between Lines A and B.

Quneitra: disengagement took effect 6 June 1974 and the town returned to Syrian civil control; a UN-commissioned report (Gruner) concluded Israeli forces deliberately destroyed it before withdrawing (almost 4,000 buildings); UNGA Res. 3240 (29 Nov 1974, 93-8-74) called it a 'grave breach' of the Fourth Geneva Convention; Israel's position: most damage occurred in the 1967 and 1973 wars and the shelling between them; the town has lain in the UNDOF zone since 1974.

Sinai I (January 1974): Israel withdrew from the western bank of the Suez Canal; Sinai II (Geneva, 4 September 1975): Israel gave up the Mitla and Gidi passes and the Abu Rudeis oil fields, with a UN-monitored buffer zone; Kissinger and Ford pressured Israel by suspending arms deliveries; the US promised not to negotiate with the PLO until it recognised Israel and accepted 242.

Bush letter to Sharon, 14 April 2004: under the plan Israel would withdraw 'certain military installations and all settlements from Gaza' and certain military installations and settlements in the West Bank; 'In light of new realities on the ground, including already existing major Israeli populations centers, it is unrealistic to expect that the outcome of final status negotiations will be a full and complete return to the armistice lines of 1949'; refugees to be settled in a Palestinian state 'rather than in Israel'.

Dov Weisglass, Sharon's senior adviser, in an interview with Ari Shavit published in Haaretz (reported 6 Oct 2004): disengagement 'supplies the amount of formaldehyde that is necessary so there will not be a political process with the Palestinians'; 'the freezing of the political process'; the Palestinian state package 'has been removed indefinitely from our agenda'; 190,000 of 240,000 settlers 'will not be moved'; the rest not dealt with 'until the Palestinians turn into Finns'.

AP (Oct 2004): Sharon's office said the prime minister remained committed to the road map; Weisglass told Israel Radio Haaretz had cut one of his quotes and said that with a broken-down PA and 'murderous Palestinian terrorism' there would be no negotiations; the Palestinian ambassador to the UN circulated the quotes as an official UN document (A/59/427, 8 Oct 2004).

21 March 2023: Knesset repealed by 31-18 the Disengagement Law clauses barring Israelis from the sites of Homesh, Ganim, Kadim and Sa-Nur, the only West Bank settlements evacuated in 2005; sponsor Yuli Edelstein (Likud); Gantz said it was 'wrong to return to northern Samaria'; Labor's Kariv called it a 'pre-annexation bill'; Sa'ar and Elkin (National Unity) backed it; ToI notes it conflicts with Israel's commitment to the Bush administration.

Olmert's 2008 offer as he described it: Israel to keep 6.3% of the West Bank for major settlements, swap Israeli land equal to 5.8% plus a Gaza link, withdraw from Arab neighbourhoods of East Jerusalem, place the Old City under international control, accept a symbolic number of refugees; Abbas did not accept: 'He showed me a map. He didn't give me a map.'

Rabin to the Knesset, 5 October 1995 (Oslo II): permanent solution 'in the framework of the State of Israel which will include most of the area of the Land of Israel'; Palestinian 'entity which is less than a state'; borders 'beyond the lines which existed before the Six-Day War. We will not return to the 4 June 1967 lines'; security border in the Jordan Valley 'in the broadest meaning of that term'; united Jerusalem including Ma'ale Adumim and Givat Ze'ev; settlement blocs; commitment 'not to uproot a single settlement' in the interim agreement.

Letters of 9 Sept 1993: Arafat: 'The PLO recognizes the right of the State of Israel to exist in peace and security' and renounces terrorism; Rabin: Israel decided 'to recognize the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people'. Declaration of Principles signed 13 Sept 1993; on 23 Sept 1993 a no-confidence motion over it failed 61-50 with 8 abstentions.

JVL Knesset highlights: the Israel-Jordan treaty was approved by 'a majority of 105' with three against and six abstaining, the day before the 26 Oct 1994 signing (conflicts with the 92-3 figure in gi8_wiki_jotreaty).

entries.topic: Israeli opposition to expansion: movements, security chiefs, parties, polling, official denials

claims.text: The Officers' Letter of 7 March 1978 to Begin, signed by 348 reserve officers and soldiers, criticised a government that 'prefers settlements beyond the Green Line to terminating the historic conflict' and said 'real security can be achieved only when we achieve peace'; it founded Peace Now; it warned of ruling around a million Arabs and jeopardising Israel's Jewish and democratic character.
Peace Now says it helped rally 400,000 people in 1982 after Sabra and Shatila to demand a commission of inquiry; its Settlement Watch project began in 1990.

Twenty-five former senior Israeli security and defence officials, including former Mossad and Shin Bet heads and three former Netanyahu advisers, wrote to Congress (letter sent 27 August 2019): 'Any unilateral annexation of territory or extension of sovereignty to the West Bank will put Israel's security and safety' at risk; backed a negotiated two-state outcome.
IDI (Israeli Voice Index, April 2020): 45% of Israelis supported applying sovereignty under the coalition agreement (52% of Jews, 9% of Arabs), 32% opposed.
INSS December 2024 (on Smotrich's sovereignty push): 21% supported annexing the entire West Bank, 21% only settlement areas, 34% opposed any annexation.

Tel Aviv University Peace Index, 26–30 July 2026: annexation of the territories with one state under Israeli rule and limited Palestinian rights — total 28% support, 59% oppose (Jews 33% support, 56% oppose); independent Palestinian state — total 32% support, 59% oppose (Jews 24% support, 68% oppose); forced choice: Jews 42% annexation vs 26% Palestinian state.
IDI, 14–18 September 2025: 70% of Israelis (78% of Jews) said a Palestinian state at this time was undesirable for Israel's national interest.

Al Jazeera, 17 Oct 2026: of the leaders seeking to replace Netanyahu, Bennett is a longtime supporter of settlements; neither Bennett nor Lapid has supported a Palestinian state; Eisenkot is not committed to one; Yair Golan's Democrats acknowledge a Palestinian state as 'a distant, unspecified goal'; no leader's position on annexation is quoted.

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, 9 Dec 2024, on the move into the Syrian buffer zone: 'This is a limited and temporary step we took for security reasons'; Netanyahu said the 1974 agreement had collapsed and Israel would not 'allow any hostile force to establish itself on our border'.

entries.topic: Israeli courts and settlement law: Regulation Law 2017-2020, Amona, Elon Moreh

claims.text: The Regulation Law passed the Knesset in February 2017, 60-52; it would retroactively legalise about 2,000 homes built on privately owned Palestinian land, transferring use rights to the Commissioner of Government Property with owners compensated above value or given alternative plots; a nine-justice panel led by Chief Justice Esther Hayut heard petitions by Palestinian local councils and left-wing groups; Justice Hendel froze it in August 2017.

The attorney general's representative Aner Helman told the court (June 2018): 'In the attorney general's opinion the Regulation Law is null and void'; Mandelblit called it 'a harmful law which would not stand up to the test of proportionality'; the government hired private attorney Harel Arnon to defend it.

9 June 2020: the High Court of Justice ruled 8-1 that the Regulation Law was unconstitutional and void; experts estimated about 4,000 settler homes on private Palestinian land; owners would have received 125% compensation. Likud called the ruling 'unfortunate' and vowed a new law; Levin: the court 'trampled on Israeli democracy'; Hotovely: 'a declaration of war on the rights of Jews to settle the Land of Israel'; Bennett urged annexation; Gantz said the law should never have passed and the ruling would be respected; Peace Now, a petitioner, welcomed it; B'Tselem said it does little to stop the settlement project.

Amona: a 2014 High Court ruling held that part of the land was Palestinian-owned; the court ordered the outpost demolished by 25 Dec 2016 and rejected relocation to an adjacent plot also privately owned; 42 families were evacuated and dismantling began 6 Feb 2017; Netanyahu ordered a new settlement to replace it, the first new official settlement in about 25 years.
